Coordinate system

Latitude and longitude from the sheet

Only needed when your sheet has grid coordinates instead of latitude and longitude. Google Earth always wants WGS84 latitude and longitude, so this is what converts your grid into it.

Every system is stored inside this program. Nothing is looked up online. The accuracy badge is how closely that grid's datum is tied to WGS84, which is what Google Earth uses. Anything worse than a metre or two is worth proving with a known mark below before you trust it.

International 1924 ellipsoid · origin 24°27′N 51°13′E · scale 0.99999 · false origin 200000 E, 300000 N · geocentric shift to WGS84 applied. Checked against 56 approved marks on this project: worst 0.09 m.

Shift to WGS84 — leave at zero if you don't have it

Negative longitudes for west, negative latitudes for south. Southern-hemisphere grids usually carry a false northing of 10000000.

Check against a known point

Type one mark whose grid and geographic values you both trust. The tool shows how far off the conversion is, and can absorb the difference so the rest of your points match your existing records.

Site calibration

not used

Tie the job to control points whose true coordinates you know. The program fits the best shift, rotation and scale from your sheet onto them, shows how well each control point agrees, and can apply the fit to every point. Works for a slightly-off national grid and for a project site grid alike.

Job profiles

nothing saved

Save the whole setup under a job name — the grid, the symbols, the photo size, the check limits — and pick it up again next month without setting any of it twice.

none

A logo has to travel inside the file, so choosing one makes the output a KMZ even when there are no photos. Google Earth opens it the same way.

Lines and areas

points only

Join the points up to draw a kerb line, a fence, a pipe run or a plot boundary. Lengths are worked out on the ground, and a closed shape gives you its area.

Choose the code of the centreline points — CL, a kerb, a pipe. Every other point then gets its chainage along that line and its offset from it, right positive, left negative.

Level profile

Type points by hand

for a few points off a level book

For the odd point that never made it into a sheet — a benchmark off a level book, a corner read from a drawing. Each one is added to the rows on the left, so everything else works on it exactly as if it had been opened from a file.

Enter moves to the next box; Enter on Remarks adds the point. The station name and both coordinates are needed — the rest is optional.

Balloon contents

every column, as read

Choose what a client sees when they click a point: tick the fields to show, move them up or down, and give them a friendlier name. ELEVATION can read Level (m), for example. The sheet itself is not changed.

Filter what is saved

everything

Save only part of the job — just the benchmarks, one row of trees, a range of point numbers. The table, the map, the checks and every saved file follow the filter.

Compare with design

nothing loaded

Load the design sheet and it is matched against what you shot, station by station. Anything outside tolerance is listed here, marked in the saved file, and carried into the report.

Quality checks

nothing checked yet

Run before you hand the file over. It looks for the mistakes that survive a visual check: the same point shot twice, a level that jumps, points on top of each other, and rows with no height.

Point symbols

one symbol for every point

Give each kind of point its own marker so a plan can be read at a glance. The tool guesses from the wording — a row saying tree gets a tree, a benchmark gets a target — and each kind becomes its own folder in Google Earth, so you can switch them on and off.

Google Earth draws labels at a fixed size on the screen, so when you zoom out they stay large while the ground shrinks, and a busy site turns into a pile of text. Labels appear holds them back until the camera comes down below the height you choose. The markers themselves always show. The height is approximate, since it depends a little on the size of the screen.

Site photos

none attached

Attach a photo of each mark and it appears inside the Google Earth balloon. The file is then saved as KMZ, which is a KML with the pictures packed inside it, so one file carries everything and works on any computer or phone.

A photo is matched to a row when its file name matches the STATION value, so TREE-01.jpg lands on the row named TREE-01. If your sheet has a PHOTO column, the name in that column is used instead.
